extracted.intended_audience: number theorists and mathematicians following the IUT/abc controversy (research mathematicians, informed readers of Mochizuki/abc)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practical criteria for assessing a claimed proof of a major result (here Mochizuki's purported proof of the abc conjecture), focusing on clarity of definitions, correctness of diagrams and maps, appropriate use of automorphisms/indeterminacies, community/refereeing norms, and exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community expert verification prior to publication
rubrics_metrics.description: It's completely unheard of for a major journal to publish a proof of an important result when experts have publicly stated that the proof is flawed and are standing behind that statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journal publication of a claimed proof of a major theorem should normally follow either community acceptance or clear resolution of expert objections. Publishing despite prominent, public expert statements that the proof is flawed is an anti-pattern and raises concerns about editorial process and trustworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid editorial conflict of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: That Mochizuki is the chief editor of the journal and that the announcement was made by two of his RIMS colleagues doesn’t help at all with the situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the author of a major claimed proof holds editorial power at the venue publishing it, readers should treat publication with caution; transparent conflict-of-interest handling and independent refereeing are required to maintain credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions must be standard, unambiguous, and accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: A falsification of the proof requires a fluency in the definitions which seems hard or impossible to achieve. Many of the definitions use nonstandard terminology and come off as ambiguous to many readers (…); these difficulties make it so that what Mochizuki has written is not a proof in traditional terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should use clear, preferably standard terminology or else provide precise, unambiguous definitions with examples. Nonstandard or ambiguous language that prevents independent checking is a serious defect. Scoring: higher clarity/standardization → easier verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors should engage with critiques and revise exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: If Mathematician A is using language that increases the risk of errors, and Mathematician A refuses to change this language, then we have found a bunch of pieces of evidence that A is the one who has made the error and not B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A willingness to clarify, rewrite, and respond to substantive technical criticisms is an important signal of reliability. Refusal to adapt or explain unusual terminology/choices increases skepticism about correctness; anti-patterns include ignoring community feedback or claiming that the peculiar style 'reduces risk' without demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: State precise hypotheses when asserting contradictions/refutations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Scholze-Stix manuscript proves: Assuming that one may identify Hodge Theaters in Mochizuki’s theory and simultaneously impose 'concrete normalizations' of q-pilot and theta-pilot degrees then there is a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both proofs and refutations must state the exact assumptions used. A claimed counterexample or contradiction is only meaningful when the hypotheses are explicit; vague or implicit hypotheses make both verification and falsification ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check algebraic/diagrammatic consistency (e.g., whether maps are ring homomorphisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: The logarithm map is not a map of rings. This is why you have to consider source and target up to some indeterminacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify that the maps and diagrams used in arguments have the algebraic properties required (commutativity, homomorphism properties, etc.). If a key map fails to be a ring map, then either the construction must account for that (via indeterminacies) or the argument fails. Anti-pattern: assuming maps have stronger structure than they do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about indeterminacies and their role
rubrics_metrics.description: Ind2 (and ind1/ind3) are used to make constructions independent of the structure that it was constructed from; ind2 has the property of 'mixing valuations' … Moral: in order for Mochizuki’s inequality to be true, you do need ind3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an argument relies on 'indeterminacies' (choices up to automorphism, poly-isomorphisms, etc.), explicitly define them (Ind1, Ind2, Ind3), show how they act, and demonstrate they suffice for the desired conclusions. Vague appeals to indeterminacy are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate objects and objects up to isomorphism without care
rubrics_metrics.description: Forgetting the history of a group you still have groups and they may still have natural commuting isomorphisms between them. Of course, for groups up to isomorphism you can’t ask for natural commuting isomorphisms between them, then you only have 'full poly-isomorphisms'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise when working 'up to isomorphism' versus choosing fixed representatives. Replacing poly-isomorphisms by fixed isomorphisms (or vice versa) without justification can change the mathematical content and lead to errors. Explain when and why such replacements are valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of techniques: identities vs inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Invariance under a group action is very useful for proving identities, but not useful for proving inequalities, unless one proves an inequality by first deriving an identity and using a separate argument to convert that identity into an inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the intended mathematical technique matches the type of claim. Do not rely on symmetry or invariance arguments intended for equalities to establish inequalities unless additional steps justify that conversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer test cases/specializations that remove confounders
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many fields F with no automorphisms that one could run the argument over, and the discrepancy vanishes there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To probe whether an argument depends on exotic automorphism phenomena, test it in special cases (e.g., base fields with no automorphisms). If the construction misbehaves even in simple/special cases, that's evidence of a problem; conversely, demonstrating correctness across representative specializations strengthens confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid psychological or rhetorical justifications in place of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: These [quoted justificatory passages] are indeed particularly weird, and reflect the psychological crutch I mentioned earlier. This is not mathematics in the slightest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments should be mathematical, not rhetorical. Appeals to how 'people will remember' or other psychological claims do not substitute for precise mathematical definitions or proofs. Treat such remarks as explanatory commentary only, not as part of the logical argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify minimal signatures and precise structures (e.g., Hodge Theaters)
rubrics_metrics.description: I certainly haven’t worked out what the signature of a Hodge Theater is but I do think this should be worked out. Every individual construction I have encountered always requires much less than the full Hodge Theater. I certainly haven’t worked out what the signature of a Hodge Theater is but I do think this should be worked out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When introducing complex/new structures, give their minimal 'signature' (what sorts of sets, relations, functions they contain) and explain which parts of that structure are used in each argument. This helps independent readers check only the needed components and reduces unnecessary complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify introduction of 'alien copies' or nonstandard constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: There is the thesis that sometimes in Mathematics one can introduce 'alien copies' of objects to prove something about your original object. This runs counter to the assumption of identifying Hodge Theaters in the above theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an argument creates multiple 'copies' of objects or works with nonstandard variants, explicitly justify the move, show how the copies relate to original objects, and demonstrate why the technique is necessary and sound. Unexplained duplication is an obstruction to checking correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid opaque presentation choices (formatting, missing TOC) that hinder reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Let’s see what the print version looks like (hopefully it has a table of contents and remove bolding and italics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readable formatting, a clear table of contents, and conventional organization materially help verification. Poor typesetting/formatting or exotic presentation that obstructs navigation is an avoidable barrier to checking a proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward clear exposition and accessible writing
rubrics_metrics.description: We should praise the writers whose writing we find 'easy' and useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, well-explained mathematical writing that makes verification feasible is valuable and should be encouraged. When assessing a work, consider exposition quality as part of its evaluative criteria: better exposition → higher likelihood of independent verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mix incompatible assumptions/propositions without checking consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: By allowing yourself to replace polyisomorphisms by fixed isomorphisms and then at the same time cite Propositions from Mochizuki this could get you in trouble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain internal consistency: if a lemma/proposition is stated under certain identification conventions (e.g., objects up to automorphism), do not reuse it as if a fixed identification were chosen unless you verify the proposition remains valid. Mixing contexts leads to invalid inferences.
